blocks.text: Almost every system needs identifiers for rows, messages, orders or URLs. On one database server this is trivial: an auto-increment column hands out 1, 2, 3… But as soon as writes are spread across many database shards or many application servers, a single counter becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure, and two shards each counting from 1 will produce collisions.
So the real question is: **how do many machines independently mint IDs that never collide, without talking to each other on every request?** Secondary requirements decide which scheme you pick:

head: Requirement
Why it matters
Who needs it
rows: Two different things must never share an ID
Sorting by ID ≈ sorting by creation time; B-tree inserts land at the end of the index
Fits a BIGINT; smaller indexes and foreign keys than 128-bit
Generation must not be a network round trip on the hot path

cols.title: Central counter (DB sequence, Redis INCR)
cons: Every ID is a network call; the counter is a SPOF and a throughput ceiling

cols.title: Range allocation (ticket server, Hi/Lo)
pros: Each server leases a block of 1,000 IDs, then generates locally
cons: Gaps when servers restart; IDs only roughly ordered across servers

cols.title: Random (UUIDv4)
pros: Zero coordination; anyone can generate offline
cons: 128 bits; random order fragments B-tree indexes; no time info

cols.title: Structured time-based (Snowflake, ULID, UUIDv7)
pros: Local generation, sortable by time, compact (64-bit Snowflake)
cons: Depends on clocks; needs unique worker ids

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd generate IDs locally with a Snowflake-style scheme: 64-bit, time-ordered, no coordination per ID — the only thing coordinated is the worker id, once at startup.

sections.title: How Snowflake works, bit by bit

blocks.text: Twitter's Snowflake packs three fields into a signed 64-bit integer. Because the timestamp occupies the most significant bits, numeric order is (approximately) creation-time order.

fields.label: timestamp
fields.sub: ms since a custom epoch ≈ 69 years

items: **Timestamp (41 bits):** milliseconds since a custom epoch (e.g. 2020-01-01). 2^41 ms ≈ 69.7 years before overflow — pick the epoch close to your launch date.
**Worker id (10 bits):** unique per generating process (often split into 5 bits datacenter + 5 bits machine). This is the only coordination: assign it once, at startup.
**Sequence (12 bits):** a per-millisecond counter on that worker; 4,096 IDs per millisecond = ~4M IDs/s per worker. If exhausted, spin until the next millisecond.

rows.label: Worker-id registry
rows.sub: ZooKeeper / etcd / DB lease — at startup only

blocks.caption: Each app server mints IDs locally; coordination happens once
Assigning a worker id at boot, then generating with zero network calls

blocks.text: Generating the ID before the insert has a practical bonus: the application knows the ID up front, so it can write to several tables, publish events and return the ID to the client without waiting for a DB round trip.

Snowflake's correctness rests on the timestamp never going backwards on a given worker. Real clocks do go backwards: NTP corrections, leap-second smearing, VM migrations. If the clock jumps back by 5 ms and the sequence resets, the worker can re-issue an ID it already issued.

head: Strategy
Behaviour
Trade-off
rows: Throw / return an error until the clock catches up
Sleep until now() > lastMs (if the skew is small, e.g. < 10 ms)
Keep using lastMs and keep incrementing the sequence (borrowing future ms)
Reserve bits for a 'clock epoch' that is bumped after a backwards jump

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Two processes accidentally sharing a worker id. They'll generate identical IDs in the same millisecond. Use a lease (with TTL and fencing) rather than a static config value, and stop generating if the lease is lost.

head: Scheme
Size
Layout
When to choose it
rows: IDs must be unguessable and ordering doesn't matter
You want UUIDs (standard column type) but time-ordered inserts
48-bit ms timestamp + 80 random bits; Crockford base32 text
Human-friendly sortable strings, no worker ids
Compact BIGINT keys at very high rates
Longer lifespan (174 years), more machines, fewer IDs per ms
41 time + 13 shard id + 10 sequence, generated in Postgres
The ID encodes which shard the row lives on

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Time-ordered IDs matter for databases: random UUIDv4 primary keys insert all over a B-tree, causing page splits and poor cache locality. UUIDv7 / ULID / Snowflake append near the right edge of the index.

items: IDs from one worker are strictly increasing.
IDs from different workers are only ordered to within clock skew (a few ms). Two events 1 ms apart on different machines may sort the wrong way round.
If you need a strict global order (a ledger, a chat channel), assign a **sequence per partition** (e.g. per channel, via the partition leader) rather than relying on ID order.
Don't expose sequential integers publicly if enumeration is a risk; expose a random or encrypted public id and keep the Snowflake internal.

head: Situation
Pick
rows: Many shards, need BIGINT and time order
Clients generate IDs offline (mobile, distributed edge)
Range-allocated counter encoded in base62, or random base62 with collision check
